taxonomy.authority_source: Kew Plants of the World Online

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew Plants of the World Online treats Texas as an introduced area; TPWD marks A. curassavica a non-native milkweed. Explicit user request for nursery/field look-alike training.

look_here_first: Check red to scarlet reflexed corolla lobes around bright yellow or orange-yellow corona hoods, then inspect the opposite, relatively smooth narrow leaves. Verify the milky latex and erect, often branched habit. Contrast with native butterfly milkweed, which has alternate hairy leaves and clear/watery sap.

morphology_keys.habit: Erect, often branching short-lived perennial or subshrub in frost-free settings; frequently grown as an annual in colder conditions; commonly about 0.3–0.9 m in Texas descriptions.
morphology_keys.sap_type: White milky latex; avoid skin or eye contact.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Leaves mainly opposite; some descriptions report whorls of three. Never infer opposite strictly from a single crowded node.
morphology_keys.leaf_morphology: Narrowly oblong to lanceolate blades, mostly 6–13 cm long, usually short-stalked, tapering/pointed at the tip; stems and leaves nearly smooth to minutely hairy.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Umbel-like clusters at upper nodes or upper leaf axils; several showy flowers per cluster.
morphology_keys.flower_color: Typically scarlet to red-orange reflexed corolla lobes contrasting with yellow to orange-yellow hooded corona; horticultural color forms can vary.
morphology_keys.gynostegium_detail: Five corona hoods are present; Kew's Cayman Islands description records erect hoods with projecting horns. Unlike the viridis/asperula pair, do not confuse the yellow hoods with the red corolla lobes.
morphology_keys.fruit: Slender spindle-shaped follicle, roughly 6–10 cm long, with comose seeds.
morphology_keys.flowering_texas: June–October noted in TPWD's guide, but cultivated plants can bloom outside that window with favorable weather.

fastest_traits: Red-orange reflexed corolla lobes, bright yellow corona hoods
Opposite narrow, mostly smooth leaf blades (occasionally apparent whorls of three)
Erect or branching habit; often nursery-grown

comparisons.distinction: Native butterfly milkweed generally has clear watery sap, alternate often hairy leaves, and orange flowers whose corolla and hood colors are less strongly bicolored. Do not use flower color alone; horticultural forms vary.
Green milkweed has broader, often blunter leaves and pale green corollas with often rose/purplish hoods, rather than scarlet corollas with yellow hoods.
Antelopehorns typically has narrow pointed leaves too, but dense pale-green/cream and purple flower heads, lower clustered stems, and is native to the focal zone.

field_diagnostics.false_positive_warning: The vernacular 'Mexican butterfly weed' may cause confusion with A. tuberosa. Use scientific names and check foliage/sap.

ecological_notes.host_status: Monarch larvae can feed on tropical milkweed; host use does not make it locally native or appropriate for restoration.
ecological_notes.conservation_caution: Where tropical milkweed stays leafy during warm winters, it can support unusual winter monarch breeding and accumulation of Ophryocystis elektroscirrha (OE) spores. Effects depend on climate and plant persistence; favor native milkweed in the natural local range (Xerces Society).
ecological_notes.texas_status: Not native to Texas. TPWD describes naturalization chiefly in southern/southeastern Texas, distinct from native-range evidence.
ecological_notes.planting_recommendation: Identification comparison only — exclude from target-zone native planting recommendations.
